edges.title: A folk poem interrupts the symphony

works.to: Urlicht; Symphony No. 2, movement IV

edges.claim: Mahler set Urlicht, a poem from the folk-poetry anthology Des Knaben Wunderhorn, before placing it between the Second Symphony’s scherzo and finale. The alto’s intimate appeal for release is a new vocal presence after three instrumental movements: the borrowed material is the poem, not a documented traditional tune.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction
sources.locator: Urlicht and the Second Symphony

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Urlicht
sources.locator: Poem and composition history

edges.title: The fish sermon loses its words

works.from: Des Knaben Wunderhorn: Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt
works.to: Des Antonius von Padua Fischpredigt; Symphony No. 2, movement III

edges.claim: In Mahler’s Wunderhorn song, Saint Anthony preaches to attentive fish who return unchanged to their usual behaviour. Its musical material also supplies the Second Symphony’s instrumental scherzo, so the poem’s circular, unsuccessful sermon has an afterlife without a singer to explain it.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction
sources.locator: Fischpredigt and Symphony No. 2

edges.title: A child’s heaven becomes the destination

works.from: Des Knaben Wunderhorn: Das himmlische Leben
works.to: Symphony No. 4, finale

edges.claim: Mahler composed Das himmlische Leben in 1892, well before the Fourth Symphony, and subsequently reorchestrated it for that work’s finale. The soprano describes a childlike heaven of food, saints and music; the apparently simple conclusion is therefore an older song around which a new symphonic destination was built.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Des Knaben Wunderhorn, introduction
sources.locator: Das himmlische Leben, 1892 and 1899–1900

edges.title: Bruckner’s Third passes through four hands

works.to: Piano-duet arrangement, 1878–1880

edges.claim: Mahler and Rudolf Krzyzanowski prepared a piano-duet arrangement of [[bruckner]]’s Third Symphony. Reducing the orchestral work to four hands was practical, detailed engagement with Bruckner’s construction, not merely admiration from a distance; the precise division of work between the two arrangers should not be treated as settled.

sources.title: Paul Banks: Gustav Mahler, arrangements
sources.locator: Bruckner, Symphony No. 3: 1878–1880

sources.title: MusicWeb International: Bruckner Third, Mahler/Krzyzanowski arrangement
sources.locator: Attribution and 1877 version

edges.title: Parsifal heard at Bayreuth

works.to: Mahler’s Bayreuth visit and letter to Fritz Löhr

edges.claim: Mahler heard Parsifal at Bayreuth in 1883 under Hermann Levi and reported the experience to Fritz Löhr. This is a documented encounter with [[wagner]]’s music in its purpose-built theatre, rather than evidence that any particular later Mahler theme was copied from it.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Gustav Mahler in Bayreuth
sources.locator: 1883 visit; Parsifal and the letter to Fritz Löhr

edges.title: Bruder Martin walks into a funeral

works.from: Bruder Martin / Frère Jacques, traditional round
works.to: Symphony No. 1, movement III, opening canon

edges.claim: Over the timpani’s tread, the First Symphony’s third movement introduces Bruder Martin, the round also known as Frère Jacques, in D minor and builds a canon from it. Mahler’s opening includes a small F–E eighth-note turn: it is not a note-for-note transcription of the familiar classroom version. Minor-mode versions of the round already circulated in Austria, so the transformation should not be advertised as Mahler’s invention.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 1, introduction
sources.locator: Third movement: Bruder Martin and Austrian minor-mode tradition

sources.title: Paul Banks: Symphony No. 1, the double-bass passage
sources.locator: 1898 score facsimile, opening of movement III

edges.title: Titan was a title, not a plot

works.to: Symphony No. 1: Hamburg programme, 1893

edges.claim: Mahler attached the name Titan, borrowed from Jean Paul’s novel, to the First Symphony for its Hamburg performance in 1893. The title does not establish a movement-by-movement setting of the novel: Mahler subsequently withdrew the programme and title, leaving a four-movement symphony.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 1, introduction
sources.locator: Hamburg 1893 and withdrawal of the programme

edges.title: Reading the symphonies beside The Brothers Karamazov

works.to: Symphonies Nos. 3 and 4

edges.claim: Celeste Belknap’s study places Mahler’s Third and Fourth Symphonies beside The Brothers Karamazov, a novel Mahler admired, especially around faith, nihilism and childhood. This offers a specific interpretative lens for the Fourth’s childlike heaven, not proof that Mahler secretly composed a Dostoevsky programme.
edges.note: Mahler’s admiration for Dostoevsky is distinct from Belknap’s proposed structural and philosophical parallels; a direct compositional dependence is not established.

sources.title: Celeste Belknap: Brothers in Philosophy: Interpreting Mahler’s Third and Fourth Symphonies through a Dostoevskian Lens
sources.locator: 2021 thesis abstract; full thesis not opened

edges.title: Rott’s scherzo: resemblance is not proof

works.to: Symphony No. 1, scherzo; comparison with Symphony No. 5

edges.claim: Hans Rott’s E-major Symphony contains Ländler-like scherzo writing that has been compared with Mahler’s First and Fifth Symphonies. Mahler knew Rott as a fellow student and later praised his music, but the securely reported loan of Rott’s score in 1900 comes after the First Symphony’s composition. Similarity, friendship and later possession of a score do not by themselves prove when Mahler first knew that passage or that he copied it.
edges.note: The musical resemblance is real enough to motivate comparison; the date and extent of Mahler’s access before composing his First Symphony remain uncertain. The edge year dates Mahler’s work, not a demonstrated act of borrowing.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Hans Rott
sources.locator: E-major Symphony; scherzo comparisons; Mahler’s 1900 score loan

edges.title: The garrison town enters the orchestra

works.from: Military bands and street music in Iglau
works.to: Mahler’s childhood listening; later marches and fanfares

edges.claim: Mahler grew up in Iglau, a Bohemian garrison town where military bands were part of everyday listening alongside church bells, synagogue music and street musicians. Michael Tilson Thomas’s Keeping Score account connects that mixed soundscape with the marches and fanfares of Mahler’s orchestral world; it does not identify every march as a quotation of a particular regimental tune.

sources.title: San Francisco Symphony / PBS: Mahler’s Origins
sources.locator: Iglau childhood soundscape

edges.title: Bach on the composing-hut desk

works.to: Mahler’s Bach study during the Hamburg years

edges.claim: Records of the Bach-Gesellschaft edition place Mahler among its subscribers during his Hamburg years, and recollections by Natalie Bauer-Lechner and Alma Mahler describe his sustained study of [[bach]]. The report that Bach scores accompanied him to his composing retreat makes this a working relationship with counterpoint, not merely a name on a list of favourite composers.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Mahler and Bach
sources.locator: Hamburg subscription, 1891–1897; Bauer-Lechner and Alma recollections

edges.title: Two Bach suites become one programme

works.to: Suite aus den Orchesterwerken von J. S. Bach

edges.claim: Mahler assembled his performing suite from movements of [[bach]]’s Second and Third Orchestral Suites. Here the connection can be followed into an actual arrangement: selected Bach movements were reorganised for Mahler’s own concert practice rather than simply imitated in a new composition.

sources.title: Paul Banks: Gustav Mahler, arrangements
sources.locator: Bach suite, 1910

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Mahler and Bach
sources.locator: Suite assembled from Orchestral Suites Nos. 2 and 3

edges.title: China reaches Mahler through several translators

works.to: Das Lied von der Erde

edges.claim: Mahler drew the texts of Das Lied von der Erde from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte, combining seven poems into six songs. Bethge’s German poems were paraphrases mediated by earlier European translations, including those of Judith Gautier and the Marquis d’Hervey-Saint-Denys, not direct translations made by Mahler from Chinese. The chain of transmission is part of the work’s history, not an inconvenience to erase.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Das Lied von der Erde, introduction
sources.locator: Bethge’s anthology and the European translation chain

edges.title: Rückert’s private grief becomes five songs

works.from: Kindertotenlieder, poems written after the deaths of two children
works.to: Kindertotenlieder, 1901–1904

edges.claim: Friedrich Rückert wrote his Kindertotenlieder after losing two children in 1833–1834; Mahler selected five poems for his song cycle. Mahler composed the settings before his own daughter Maria died in 1907, so the cycle is neither a diary of that later loss nor evidence of supernatural prediction.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Friedrich Rückert
sources.locator: Rückert’s bereavements and Mahler’s five settings, 1901–1904

edges.title: A memorial service unlocks the finale

works.to: Symphony No. 2, finale

edges.claim: At the memorial service for Hans von Bülow in 1894, Mahler heard Klopstock’s resurrection hymn and found the textual starting point for his Second Symphony’s finale. He did not simply set the complete hymn: his finale joins part of Klopstock’s poem to verses of his own.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Hans von Bülow
sources.locator: Memorial-service account and the Second Symphony’s finale

edges.title: Faust answers Veni creator spiritus

works.to: Symphony No. 8, Part II

edges.claim: The Eighth Symphony’s second part sets the closing scene of Goethe’s Faust II, following a first part built on the Latin hymn Veni creator spiritus. Mahler links these apparently distant texts through returning musical material, making Goethe’s final ascent the continuation of the opening invocation rather than a separate cantata appended to it.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 8, introduction
sources.locator: Two texts and shared thematic material

edges.title: Zarathustra sings at midnight

works.to: Symphony No. 3, movement IV

edges.claim: After three instrumental movements, the Third Symphony introduces an alto singing Nietzsche’s midnight poem from Also sprach Zarathustra. The sparse, slow setting changes the scale of listening from the preceding orchestral world to a single voice contemplating sorrow and eternity; this is an actual text setting, not a claim that the whole symphony illustrates Nietzsche’s philosophy.

sources.title: Mahler Foundation: Symphony No. 3, movement IV
sources.locator: Nietzsche’s Midnight Song and the alto setting

edges.title: Mahler’s orchestra behind Berg’s three pieces

works.to: Three Pieces for Orchestra, Op. 6

edges.claim: Mark DeVoto’s account identifies Mahler’s Ninth as a profound influence on [[berg]]’s Three Pieces for Orchestra, composed in 1914–1915. The central Reigen turns around dance material including a Ländler, while the final Marsch magnifies the orchestra into a destructive march: the inheritance is a way of organising orchestral drama, not a single asserted quotation.

sources.title: Mark DeVoto / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Berg, Three Pieces for Orchestra
sources.locator: Mahler’s Ninth; Reigen and Marsch; composition in 1914–1915

edges.title: Teenage Britten hears Mahler’s Fourth

works.to: Britten’s diary; early orchestral work including Plymouth Town

edges.claim: The teenage [[britten]] heard Mahler’s Fourth at a London Prom in September 1930 and recorded a response that combined impatience at its length with admiration for its beauty. David Matthews relates this encounter, and Britten’s subsequent purchase of the Lieder eines fahrenden Gesellen score, to the Mahlerian orchestral world of Plymouth Town; the diary establishes the encounter more securely than any proposed bar-by-bar borrowing.

sources.title: David Matthews: London, Royal College of Music: Britten’s Plymouth Town, Tempo 58/230 (2004)
sources.locator: pp. 57–58, Britten’s 1930 diary and 1931 score purchase

edges.title: Zverev’s household was also a conservatory

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s Moscow training, from 1885

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff entered Nikolai Zverev’s Moscow household as a piano pupil in 1885. Its musical gatherings also brought him into contact with [[tchaikovsky]], so the teacher provided both intensive pianistic training and access to the professional circle in which the young composer was first heard.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Zverev’s household and musical soirées, 1885 onwards

edges.title: A cousin takes over the piano lessons

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s senior Moscow studies

edges.claim: In 1888 Rachmaninoff moved into the senior stage of his Moscow Conservatory training and studied piano with his cousin Alexander Siloti. This pianistic relationship ran alongside, rather than replaced, the separate composition and counterpoint instruction he received from Arensky and Taneyev.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Senior studies from 1888

edges.title: Tchaikovsky recommends advanced counterpoint

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s Moscow Conservatory studies

edges.claim: On [[tchaikovsky]]’s recommendation, Rachmaninoff studied advanced counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev. Naming the subject matters: this was technical training in combining independent voices, not simply a vague personal influence attributed retrospectively to an older Russian master.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Taneyev and Tchaikovsky’s recommendation

edges.title: Arensky teaches the composer’s working tools

works.from: Anton Arensky’s harmony, instrumentation and composition classes
works.to: Rachmaninoff’s Moscow Conservatory studies

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff’s senior Moscow studies included composition, harmony and instrumentation with Anton Arensky. Arensky’s place in this history is therefore an identifiable teaching relationship, distinct from Taneyev’s counterpoint lessons and Siloti’s piano instruction.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Arensky’s subjects in the senior course

edges.title: Tchaikovsky champions the graduation opera

works.from: Tchaikovsky’s support and proposed Iolanta double bill
works.to: Aleko, composed 1892; Bolshoi premiere, 1893

edges.claim: [[tchaikovsky]] publicly praised Rachmaninoff’s graduation opera Aleko, attended its Bolshoi premiere in 1893 and proposed pairing it with his own Iolanta. This was concrete patronage of a younger composer’s work, not simply a later listener’s comparison of their melodies.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: December 1892 interview; Aleko premiere, 27 April/9 May 1893; Iolanta proposal

edges.title: A memorial trio answers a memorial trio

works.from: Piano Trio in A minor, Op. 50, in memory of Nikolai Rubinstein
works.to: Trio élégiaque No. 2 in D minor, Op. 9

edges.claim: After [[tchaikovsky]]’s death, Rachmaninoff composed his Second Trio élégiaque in his memory, completing it in December 1893. The choice of a large piano trio as a memorial follows the precedent of Tchaikovsky’s own trio for Nikolai Rubinstein: the younger composer mourned his patron in a form that patron had already made commemorative.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Trio élégiaque No. 2, completion 15/27 December 1893

edges.title: Grieg provides a concerto starting point

works.from: Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 16
works.to: Piano Concerto No. 1 in F-sharp minor, Op. 1, original version

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff used Grieg’s concerto as a model while composing the original version of his First Piano Concerto in 1891. This belongs to the student work’s genesis; it should not obscure how extensively Rachmaninoff later revised his own concerto in 1917.

sources.title: Tchaikovsky Research: Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: First Piano Concerto, Grieg model and later revision

edges.title: Dies irae crosses the dark water

works.to: The Isle of the Dead, Op. 29

edges.claim: In The Isle of the Dead, Rachmaninoff quotes both fragments and fuller statements of Dies irae. The medieval death chant and the painting are different kinds of source: one supplies recognisable musical material, the other the visual stimulus for the work.

sources.title: Timothy Judd: Rachmaninov’s Isle of the Dead: A Tone Poem in Black and White
sources.locator: Dies irae fragments and statements

edges.title: The death chant interrupts Paganini

works.to: Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, Op. 43, variation VII

edges.claim: Variation VII of the Paganini Rhapsody brings Dies irae into a work nominally based on a violin caprice. The piano’s chant meets fragments of Paganini’s theme in bassoons and pizzicato cellos, letting the listener hear two inherited materials interacting rather than treating the rhapsody as twenty-four independent decorations.

sources.title: Calvin Dotsey / Houston Symphony: Rachmaninoff’s Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini
sources.locator: 7 March 2025; variation VII

edges.title: Dies irae returns in the last dance

works.to: Symphonic Dances, Op. 45, movement III

edges.claim: The final Symphonic Dance repeatedly invokes Dies irae, returning to a melody Rachmaninoff had already used in The Isle of the Dead and the Paganini Rhapsody. It is set against music recalled from his own All-Night Vigil, turning the movement into an encounter between a Western death chant and his Russian sacred repertory.

sources.title: Harlow Robinson / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Rachmaninoff, Symphonic Dances
sources.locator: Movement III: Dies irae and All-Night Vigil quotation

edges.title: Old chant becomes a choral orchestra

works.to: All-Night Vigil, Op. 37, including Nos. 8 and 12

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff’s All-Night Vigil incorporates inherited Orthodox chants rather than inventing all its melodies in an antique style. David Bray’s account identifies Znamenny chant in movements including No. 8, where altos and basses carry it in octaves, and No. 12; the surrounding choral texture gives a monodic tradition a many-voiced setting.

sources.title: David Bray: Rachmaninoff Vespers, Signum SIGCD054 booklet
sources.locator: Booklet pp. 4–7; Znamenny tradition and movements 8 and 12

edges.title: The Vigil’s Alleluia survives in exile

works.from: All-Night Vigil, Op. 37, No. 9, based on Znamenny chant
works.to: Symphonic Dances, Op. 45, movement III, coda

edges.claim: Near the end of the Symphonic Dances, Rachmaninoff recalls the ninth movement of his All-Night Vigil and marks the passage with an Alleluia indication. The Russian sacred melody reaches the orchestral work through his own earlier choral setting: it is both inherited chant and self-quotation.

sources.title: Harlow Robinson / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Rachmaninoff, Symphonic Dances
sources.locator: Final movement’s quotation of Vigil No. 9 and Alleluia marking

edges.title: Böcklin’s island becomes a symphonic poem

works.from: Die Toteninsel / Isle of the Dead, series of paintings
works.to: The Isle of the Dead, Op. 29

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff’s encounter with a black-and-white reproduction of Arnold Böcklin’s Isle of the Dead stimulated his tone poem; he later found the painting in colour less compelling than the reproduction. The music’s recurring 5/8 motion accompanies an imagined crossing towards the island, but the illustration here is identified as a particular version, not asserted to be the exact reproduction he saw.

sources.title: Timothy Judd: Rachmaninov’s Isle of the Dead: A Tone Poem in Black and White
sources.locator: 1907 reproduction encounter and the tone poem

edges.title: Chopin’s miniature becomes twenty-two variations

works.from: Prelude in C minor, Op. 28 No. 20
works.to: Variations on a Theme of Chopin, Op. 22

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff chose [[chopin]]’s C-minor Prelude as the theme for twenty-two piano variations, written in 1902–1903. The excerpts isolate the opening upper voice of Chopin’s chordal theme and its restatement by Rachmaninoff; hearing that plain outline first makes the later virtuoso transformations easier to follow.

edges.title: The pianist writes inside Liszt’s rhapsody

works.to: Rachmaninoff’s cadenza, documented in a concert programme of 23 January 1919

edges.claim: By January 1919, Rachmaninoff was performing [[liszt]]’s Second Hungarian Rhapsody with his own cadenza, explicitly identified in a Carnegie Hall programme. This is a particularly literal meeting of pianist-composers: rather than merely adopting a virtuoso manner, Rachmaninoff inserted newly composed material into his performance of an older pianist-composer’s work.

edges.title: Paganini’s theme arrives after its first variation

works.from: Caprice No. 24 in A minor, Op. 1
works.to: Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini, Op. 43

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff built his Rhapsody on the theme of Paganini’s Twenty-fourth Caprice, but placed a skeletal first variation before the theme itself. The famous eighteenth variation later turns the theme upside down and into the major mode: its lyricism is a transformation of the same source, not an unrelated tune dropped into the work.

edges.title: Poe’s bells arrive through Balmont

works.from: The Bells, in Konstantin Balmont’s Russian adaptation
works.to: The Bells, Op. 35

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff’s choral symphony The Bells sets Konstantin Balmont’s free Russian adaptation of Poe, not Poe’s English poem directly. Its four movements pass through sleigh bells, wedding bells, alarm bells and funeral bells; Balmont’s changes, including an earlier presence of death, are part of the text Rachmaninoff actually composed.

sources.title: Robert McColley / American Symphony Orchestra: The Bells, Sergei Rachmaninoff
sources.locator: Poe, Balmont and the four-movement text

edges.title: Mahler rehearses Rachmaninoff’s Third

works.to: Piano Concerto No. 3, January 1910 performances

edges.claim: [[mahler]] conducted Rachmaninoff as soloist in the Third Piano Concerto in New York in January 1910, after its premiere under Walter Damrosch. Rachmaninoff later singled out Mahler’s painstaking rehearsal work: this connection between two favourites is documented collaboration over a new score, not a hypothetical stylistic resemblance.

sources.title: New Mexico Philharmonic: Rachmaninoff & Ravel programme notes
sources.locator: Third Piano Concerto: Damrosch premiere and Mahler performances

edges.title: Fauré’s classroom hears the young Ravel

works.to: Ravel’s studies; early Sonata for violin and piano

edges.claim: Ravel studied composition with [[faure]] from 1897, and his early single-movement violin sonata belongs to that classroom world. Bru Zane identifies a probable performance in Fauré’s class in 1897–1898 and hears the older composer’s chamber-music example in it; the classroom performance is reported as probable, not certain.

sources.title: Bru Zane Mediabase: Ravel, Sonata no. 1 for piano and violin
sources.locator: Composition class, probable 1897–1898 performance and stylistic models

sources.locator: 1897 return to the Conservatoire; Fauré and Gédalge

edges.title: Gédalge teaches the contrapuntal craft

works.to: Ravel’s Conservatoire-period training

edges.claim: Alongside Fauré’s composition class, Ravel took private counterpoint lessons with André Gédalge. Keeping the two teachers distinct avoids attributing every part of Ravel’s technical education to Fauré alone: Gédalge supplied a separate, specifically contrapuntal apprenticeship.

sources.title: Maurice Ravel: biography and Conservatoire studies
sources.locator: 1897 studies with Fauré and private counterpoint with Gédalge

edges.title: Chabrier behind the grotesque serenade

works.to: Sérénade grotesque

edges.claim: In his autobiographical account, Ravel explicitly associated his early Sérénade grotesque with Chabrier’s influence. This is the composer identifying a model for a particular piece, a stronger connection than a later critic hearing a general family likeness between two French piano styles.

sources.title: Peter Jost / Henle: Between distance and admiration: Satie and Ravel
sources.locator: 14 July 2025; Ravel’s retrospective account of the two early pieces

edges.title: Ravel names Satie as an early model

works.to: Ballade de la reine morte d’aimer

edges.claim: Ravel’s autobiographical sketch names [[satie]] as an influence on the early Ballade de la reine morte d’aimer. The piece is not available for a reliable musical comparison, so the evidence here is Ravel’s own retrospective statement rather than a reconstructed passage or an invented quotation.

sources.title: Peter Jost / Henle: Between distance and admiration: Satie and Ravel
sources.locator: Ravel’s autobiographical sketch and the Ballade

edges.title: The Pavane’s Satie-like wrong-note chords

works.to: Pavane pour une infante défunte, original piano version

edges.claim: Peter Jost compares the Pavane’s calmly sustained dissonances and unexpected bass support with [[satie]]’s early piano writing. This is a harmonic comparison, not a claim that Ravel copied the Gymnopédie melody; the excerpt isolates Ravel’s tune so that the listener can distinguish melody from the accompaniment where the proposed resemblance lies.
edges.note: Jost’s analytical comparison does not establish a particular Satie passage as a consciously borrowed source for the Pavane.

edges.title: Poe offers a method, not a programme

works.from: The Philosophy of Composition, through Baudelaire’s translations
works.to: Ravel’s account of his compositional method

edges.claim: Ravel identified Poe’s The Philosophy of Composition as an important guide to his thinking about making a work. Emily Kilpatrick places that reading beside Ravel’s concern with deliberate construction and artistic originality; it is evidence about a declared method, not permission to attach a hidden Poe story to every instrumental score.

edges.title: Pictures gains a saxophone and an orchestra

works.from: Pictures at an Exhibition, piano suite, 1874
works.to: Pictures at an Exhibition, orchestration, 1922

edges.claim: Serge Koussevitzky commissioned Ravel’s orchestration of [[mussorgsky]]’s piano Pictures at an Exhibition, first performed in Paris in October 1922. The trumpet’s opening Promenade and the alto saxophone of The Old Castle are Ravel’s instrumental decisions: the melodies and suite belong to Mussorgsky, while the familiar orchestral colours belong to the arranger.

sources.title: Michael Steinberg / Boston Symphony Orchestra: Pictures at an Exhibition
sources.locator: Koussevitzky commission, 22 October 1922 premiere and instrumentation

edges.title: An old French suite mourns modern soldiers

works.from: Couperin and the French keyboard-suite tradition
works.to: Le Tombeau de Couperin, piano suite, 1914–1917

edges.claim: Le Tombeau de Couperin invokes the older French keyboard tradition rather than quoting a single identified [[couperin]] work. Ravel gave its movements separate memorial dedications to men killed in the First World War; the Toccata remembers Joseph de Marliave, whose widow Marguerite Long gave the complete suite’s premiere in 1919.

sources.title: Jillian Rogers: Mourning at the Piano: Marguerite Long, Maurice Ravel, and the Performance of Grief

edges.title: Spanish songs remembered from his mother

works.from: Spanish songs sung by Ravel’s mother
works.to: Ravel’s Spanish musical world, including Rapsodie espagnole

edges.claim: Ravel’s mother sang Spanish songs to him, giving his later fascination with Spain a family setting as well as a concert-hall one. The connection helps explain why Spanish subjects recur in his music, including Rapsodie espagnole; it does not identify every ostensibly Spanish melody as an actual childhood song quotation.

sources.title: Los Angeles Philharmonic: Get to Know Ravel
sources.locator: Ravel’s mother and Spanish songs

sources.locator: Family origins and Spanish musical affinities

edges.title: The Trio sways in three-two-three

works.to: Piano Trio in A minor, movement I

edges.claim: The first movement of Ravel’s Piano Trio groups its eight eighth notes as 3 + 2 + 3, a rhythm the Library of Congress programme note connects with Basque dance. Listen for unequal lengths rather than a conventional four-square pulse: the regional connection is rhythmic and need not imply a verbatim folk-tune quotation.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Beaux Arts Trio Farewell Concert, Ravel Trio programme note
sources.locator: Ravel Trio: first movement’s 8/8 grouped 3 + 2 + 3

edges.title: Ravel’s Blues predates the American tour

works.to: Sonata for violin and piano, movement II, Blues

edges.claim: Ravel called the middle movement of his 1927 violin sonata Blues, before his celebrated American visit and meeting with Gershwin in 1928. The chronology matters: American music was already a compositional resource for him, not a revelation that began at Gershwin’s piano in New York.

sources.title: Jack Zimmerman / Chicago Symphony Orchestra: Fascinatin’ Rhythm: When Ravel met Gershwin
sources.locator: 1927 Blues and the 1928 American tour

edges.title: Gershwin plays at Ravel’s birthday party

works.from: Rhapsody in Blue and The Man I Love
works.to: Ravel’s New York encounter with Gershwin, 7 March 1928

edges.claim: At Éva Gauthier’s New York party for Ravel’s birthday on 7 March 1928, [[gershwin]] played music including Rhapsody in Blue and The Man I Love. The meeting is well documented, but it did not make Gershwin Ravel’s pupil; colourful versions of the refused-lessons anecdote should not be mistaken for a completed course of instruction.

sources.title: Jack Zimmerman / Chicago Symphony Orchestra: Fascinatin’ Rhythm: When Ravel met Gershwin
sources.locator: Éva Gauthier party, 7 March 1928, and her account of the proposed lessons

edges.title: Russian orchestral colour reaches Paris

works.from: Rimsky-Korsakov’s music at the Paris Exposition
works.to: Ravel’s youthful orchestral listening

edges.claim: Ravel heard Russian music associated with [[rimsky-korsakov]] at the Paris Exposition of 1889. This gives a dated encounter behind his interest in Russian orchestral colour; it does not prove that a particular instrument in a later Ravel score was copied from a particular Rimsky-Korsakov bar.

sources.title: Maurice Ravel: early career and the 1889 Exposition
sources.locator: 1889 Exposition: Rimsky-Korsakov and Russian music

edges.title: Gaspard renews Lisztian virtuosity

works.to: Gaspard de la nuit, especially Scarbo

edges.claim: Emily Kilpatrick places Gaspard de la nuit in the virtuoso pianist-composer tradition of [[liszt]], with Scarbo as a particularly conspicuous example. The relationship concerns how extreme keyboard technique becomes a dramatic resource; it is not a verified quotation from a named Liszt composition.
edges.note: This is a scholarly account of a technical and aesthetic lineage, not a documented bar-level borrowing.

sources.title: Emily Kilpatrick: Maurice Ravel and the Poetics of Originality, 1907–14
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript, pp. 11–12: virtuoso tradition and Scarbo

edges.title: Scarbo aims beyond Islamey

works.to: Gaspard de la nuit: Scarbo

edges.claim: Ravel’s stated ambition for Scarbo was to go beyond the technical difficulty of Balakirev’s Islamey. The Russian work functions here as a challenge to surpass, not a theme to quote: repeated notes, leaps and rapid transformations become means of conjuring Bertrand’s elusive goblin.

sources.title: Emily Kilpatrick: Maurice Ravel and the Poetics of Originality, 1907–14
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript, p. 11; Ravel’s Islamey ambition, citing Orenstein

edges.title: Three prose poems become piano scenes

works.from: Gaspard de la nuit: Ondine, Le Gibet and Scarbo
works.to: Gaspard de la nuit, three poems for piano

edges.claim: Ravel printed Aloysius Bertrand’s prose poems with the three movements of Gaspard de la nuit. Ondine, Le Gibet and Scarbo therefore have specific textual companions, from the water spirit’s address to the tolling bell and the disappearing goblin; the poems are not programmes invented by later annotators.

edges.title: Schubert lends two waltz titles

works.to: Valses nobles et sentimentales

edges.claim: Ravel explicitly linked the title Valses nobles et sentimentales with [[schubert]]’s two named waltz collections. The title establishes a conscious historical conversation, but it is not evidence that Ravel’s harmonically abrasive waltzes reproduce a particular Schubert melody.

sources.title: Emily Kilpatrick: Maurice Ravel and the Poetics of Originality, 1907–14
sources.locator: Accepted manuscript, p. 4: Ravel’s statement about Schubert and the title

edges.title: Vaughan Williams comes to Paris for clarity

works.from: Ravel’s lessons in composition and orchestral craft
works.to: Vaughan Williams’s Paris study, 1907–1908

edges.claim: Ralph Vaughan Williams studied with Ravel in Paris for about three months in 1907–1908. Tom Service’s account of the surviving correspondence describes lessons directed at craft and clarity, including work with a Mozart minuet; the encounter did not require Vaughan Williams to abandon his own musical identity and become a French imitator.

sources.title: Tom Service: How Ravel helped Vaughan Williams find his voice
sources.locator: Paris lessons and British Library correspondence

edges.title: Rimsky’s crowded orchestration classroom

works.from: Rimsky-Korsakov’s St Petersburg Conservatory orchestration classes
works.to: Prokofiev’s student training

edges.claim: Prokofiev studied orchestration in [[rimsky-korsakov]]’s classes at the St Petersburg Conservatory. David Nice’s publisher biography also records his dissatisfaction with their crowded conditions, an important qualification to the easy picture of an intimate, contented master-and-disciple relationship.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 10, biography: 1906 entry

edges.title: Lyadov’s rules meet an impatient modernist

works.from: Anatoly Lyadov’s harmony and counterpoint teaching
works.to: Prokofiev’s St Petersburg Conservatory studies

edges.claim: Prokofiev studied harmony and counterpoint with Anatoly Lyadov, whose teaching he found uninspiring. The publisher’s chronology records Lyadov’s alarm at the Scriabinesque tendencies of his pupil’s 1909 examination pieces: this was instruction accompanied by aesthetic friction, not agreement about what new music should sound like.

edges.title: Conducting lessons plant the Classical Symphony

works.from: Nikolai Tcherepnin’s conducting classes and Haydn/Mozart study
works.to: Prokofiev’s training; Piano Concerto No. 1 dedication

edges.claim: Nikolai Tcherepnin taught Prokofiev conducting and encouraged his close study of Haydn and Mozart. Prokofiev dedicated his First Piano Concerto to him, while the Tcherepnin Society’s account connects those classical studies with the later conception of the Classical Symphony.

edges.title: Glière visits the child composer at home

works.to: Prokofiev’s lessons at Sontsovka, 1902–1903

edges.claim: Before the St Petersburg Conservatory, Prokofiev received two summers of teaching from Reinhold Glière at Sontsovka. Taneyev’s recommendation helped arrange the lessons, giving the child composer a concrete route from home composition towards systematic professional training.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: p. 10, 1902 entry

edges.title: Haydn’s orchestra, with modern wrong turns

works.from: Haydn’s symphonic style and orchestral practice
works.to: Symphony No. 1 in D major, Op. 25, Classical

edges.claim: Prokofiev imagined how [[haydn]] might compose in the modern world when making his Classical Symphony in 1916–1917. A compact orchestra, four-movement outline and lucid textures supply the historical frame, while abrupt harmonic turns prevent it from becoming an anonymous eighteenth-century imitation; the third movement is a gavotte rather than Haydn’s usual minuet.

edges.title: Diaghilev rejects one ballet and orders another

works.to: Ala et Lolly; Chout; Scythian Suite

edges.claim: Diaghilev commissioned Ala et Lolly after meeting Prokofiev in 1914, then rejected the result and commissioned the Russian folk-tale ballet Chout instead. Prokofiev salvaged music from the rejected project as the Scythian Suite, so the impresario’s refusal helped redirect rather than simply terminate the material’s life.

sources.locator: p. 11, 1914–1916 chronology

edges.title: A piano audition turns into a quarrel

works.to: The Love for Three Oranges and Prokofiev’s response

edges.claim: At a 1922 piano presentation of The Love for Three Oranges for Diaghilev, [[stravinsky]] objected to the opera and the two composers quarrelled. The episode records rivalry and disagreement, not a securely demonstrated musical borrowing; their relationship also included earlier collaboration at the piano, playing Petrushka together.

edges.title: Film follows music; music follows film

works.to: Alexander Nevsky film score; concert cantata, Op. 78

edges.claim: For Alexander Nevsky, Eisenstein and Prokofiev worked in both directions: some images were shaped to music, while some music was written to images. Prokofiev subsequently recast the 1938 film score as a 1939 concert cantata, so the familiar concert work is an adaptation of a collaborative audiovisual construction, not the film soundtrack unchanged.

edges.title: Romeo and Juliet nearly survived the ballet

works.to: Romeo and Juliet, ballet, Op. 64

edges.claim: Prokofiev’s 1935 ballet project initially allowed Romeo to arrive in time and the lovers to survive, before the ending was changed back to Shakespeare’s tragedy. The adaptation was therefore not inevitable note-for-note storytelling: its authors actively negotiated what a Shakespearean ending should become on the ballet stage.

sources.title: Jim Svejda / Los Angeles Philharmonic: Romeo and Juliet, complete ballet, Op. 64
sources.locator: 1935 composition and the abandoned happy ending

edges.title: Prokofiev’s Onegin is not Tchaikovsky’s opera

works.to: Eugene Onegin, incidental music, Op. 71

edges.claim: Prokofiev wrote Eugene Onegin music for Alexander Tairov’s planned stage production in 1936, using spoken voices with orchestra. The production was cancelled, leaving a substantial Pushkin adaptation that should not be confused with [[tchaikovsky]]’s opera of the same name.

sources.title: Wise Music Classical: Prokofiev, Eugene Onegin, Op. 71
sources.locator: 1936 Tairov commission, spoken forces and cancelled production

edges.title: Christian Science enters the composer’s own account

works.from: Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures; Christian Science teaching
works.to: Prokofiev’s diaries and 31 January 1933 letter to Eve Crain

edges.claim: Prokofiev’s diaries document his engagement with Christian Science from 1924, including reading Mary Baker Eddy’s Science and Health. In a 1933 letter preserved by the Mary Baker Eddy Library, he connected that faith with his work as a composer; this establishes a stated intellectual and spiritual influence, not a demonstrable source for particular harmonies or a claim that religious practice cured an illness.

sources.title: Mary Baker Eddy Library: From the Collections: Sergei Prokofiev and Christian Science
sources.locator: 1924 diary entries; facsimile and transcription of 31 January 1933 letter

edges.title: Dostoevsky’s obsession becomes an opera

works.to: The Gambler, opera, Op. 24, 1915–1917; revised 1927–1928

edges.claim: Prokofiev made Dostoevsky’s The Gambler into an opera during 1915–1917 and revised it a decade later. Unlike a conjectural literary influence on an instrumental score, the novel supplies the named dramatic source; its first planned production fell through while Prokofiev was still in Russia.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: pp. 4 and 11–13, Dostoevsky source, composition and abandoned production

edges.title: Tolstoy’s invasion meets a second invasion

works.to: War and Peace, opera, Op. 91, begun 1941

edges.claim: Prokofiev turned to Tolstoy’s War and Peace as an operatic project after the German invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941. His work with Mira Mendelson selected scenes from the novel rather than attempting to reproduce the entire book, and repeated revisions made the opera a continuing project rather than a score fixed once in 1941.

sources.title: David Nice / Boosey & Hawkes: Serge Prokofieff Work List
sources.locator: pp. 4 and 14–16, Tolstoy source and 1941–1953 chronology

edges.title: Rachmaninoff’s Corelli theme is the older Folia

works.from: Corelli, Sonata Op. 5 No. 12, Follia (1700), inherited theme
works.to: Variations on a Theme of Corelli, Op. 42 (1931)

edges.claim: Rachmaninoff’s Op. 42, composed in May and June 1931, takes its theme from the Folia familiar through Corelli’s Op. 5 finale. The title names an important transmitter rather than the tune’s inventor: the theme was already older than Corelli.
edges.note: Kreisler has often been proposed as the intermediary, but the cited critical discussion also notes Rachmaninoff’s familiarity with Liszt’s Rhapsodie espagnole. Neither route is asserted here as established.

sources.title: Norbert Gertsch, Henle: Corelli, La Folia and Rachmaninoff’s Variations, Op. 42
sources.locator: Rachmaninoff’s May–June 1931 composition, Folia ancestry, and uncertain Kreisler/Liszt transmission
